subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Competition Act, 2002 was enacted on the recommendations of a committee appointed in October 1999, and it replaced-

options.A: the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969
options.B: the Consumer Protection Act, so far as it dealt with trade
options.C: the Companies Act, 1956, so far as it dealt with monopolies
options.D: the Essential Commodities Act and the rules made under it

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969.

The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969 was the first enactment to deal with competition issues and came into effect on 1 June 1970. A committee appointed in October 1999 was asked to examine it with a view to shifting the focus of the law from curbing monopolies to promoting competition, and the Competition Act, 2002 was enacted on 13 January 2003 in consequence. The Act provides for the repeal of the MRTP Act and the dissolution of the MRTP Commission.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: An association of producers, sellers, distributors, traders or service providers who, by agreement amongst themselves, limit, control or attempt to control the production, distribution, sale or price of goods or the provision of services is-

options.A: an enterprise
options.B: a cartel
options.C: an acquisition
options.D: a combination

answer_html:
Answer: (B) a cartel.

That is the definition of a cartel. An acquisition means directly or indirectly acquiring or agreeing to acquire shares, voting rights or assets of an enterprise, or control over its management or assets. A combination is the acquisition of one or more enterprises, or a merger or amalgamation, where the prescribed thresholds are exceeded. An enterprise is a person or a department of the Government engaged in the activities described in the Act, other than the sovereign functions of the Government.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The sale of goods or the provision of services at a price below the cost of production, with a view to reducing competition or eliminating competitors, is-

options.A: discriminatory pricing
options.B: resale price maintenance
options.C: introductory pricing
options.D: predatory pricing

answer_html:
Answer: (D) predatory pricing.

Predatory price means the sale of goods or provision of services at a price below the cost of production, as may be determined by regulations, with a view to reducing competition or eliminating the competitors. Imposing an unfair or discriminatory price in the purchase or sale of goods or services, including a predatory price, is one of the ways in which a dominant position may be abused.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The difference between a horizontal agreement and a vertical agreement is that-

options.A: in a horizontal agreement the parties are at the same level of competition, while in a vertical agreement they are at different levels
options.B: in a horizontal agreement the parties are at different levels of competition, while in a vertical agreement they are at the same level
options.C: a horizontal agreement must be in writing, while a vertical agreement may be oral or inferred from the conduct of the parties
options.D: a horizontal agreement is void only if it is proved to be harmful, while a vertical agreement is void from the moment it is made

answer_html:
Answer: (A) in a horizontal agreement the parties are at the same level of competition, while in a vertical agreement they are at different levels.

In a horizontal agreement there is the same level of competition, and in a vertical agreement a different level. Vertical agreements are those entered into amongst enterprises or persons at different stages of the production and distribution chain. Agreement itself is widely defined in Section 2(b) to include any arrangement, understanding or action in concert, whether or not formal, in writing, or intended to be legally enforceable.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following is NOT a vertical agreement under the Act?

options.A: A tie-in arrangement requiring a purchaser of goods to purchase some other goods
options.B: An exclusive supply agreement restricting the purchaser from dealing in other goods
options.C: Resale price maintenance stipulating the price at which the purchaser may resell
options.D: Bid rigging or collusive bidding between enterprises engaged in a similar trade of goods

answer_html:
Answer: (D) Bid rigging or collusive bidding between enterprises engaged in a similar trade of goods.

Bid rigging or collusive bidding is one of the categories in Section 3(3), which deals with agreements between enterprises engaged in identical or similar trade, that is with horizontal agreements. Bid rigging means any agreement eliminating or reducing competition for bids or adversely affecting or manipulating the bidding process, joint venture business agreements being excepted. Tie-in arrangements, exclusive supply agreements, exclusive distribution agreements, refusal to deal and resale price maintenance are the vertical categories.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The restrictions on anti-competitive agreements do not apply to-

options.A: the right to restrain an infringement of intellectual property rights, and the right to export goods from India
options.B: an agreement between enterprises which belong to the same group of companies and carry on business in India
options.C: an agreement approved in advance by the Central Government by a notification published in the Official Gazette
options.D: an agreement to which a public financial institution or a foreign institutional investor happens to be a party

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the right to restrain an infringement of intellectual property rights, and the right to export goods from India.

The restriction does not apply to the right of any person to restrain an infringement of intellectual property rights conferred under the Copyright, Patents, Trade Marks, Geographical Indications, Designs and Semi-conductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design legislation, nor to the right of any person to export goods from India to the extent that the agreement relates exclusively to production, supply, distribution or control of goods or provision of services for such export.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: A dominant position means a position of strength enjoyed by an enterprise in the relevant market in India which enables it to-

options.A: prevent any new enterprise from entering the relevant market for a period of at least one year from the date on which entry is attempted
options.B: operate independently of the competitive forces prevailing in the relevant market, or affect its competitors, consumers or that market in its favour
options.C: secure a market share of more than one half of the relevant market, whether that share is measured by turnover or by the volume of goods sold
options.D: fix the price of its goods or services without regard to the price at which its nearest competitor in the relevant market sells the same goods

answer_html:
Answer: (B) operate independently of the competitive forces prevailing in the relevant market, or affect its competitors, consumers or that market in its favour.

Dominant position means a position of strength enjoyed by an enterprise in the relevant market in India which enables it to operate independently of the competitive forces prevailing in that market, or to affect its competitors or consumers or the relevant market in its favour. The Act does not fix any percentage of market share; market share is only one of the factors the Commission takes into account, along with size and resources, the size and importance of competitors, economic power, vertical integration, entry barriers and others.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
Nilagiri Alloys Limited proposes to merge with Konkan Steel Products Limited. Both companies carry on business only in India and neither has any assets or any turnover outside India.

On the merger the combined assets of the two enterprises in India would be ₹2,400 crore and their combined turnover in India would be ₹5,200 crore.

The group to which the merged enterprise would belong after the merger would have assets in India of ₹7,600 crore and turnover in India of ₹25,200 crore.

The board of directors of each of the two companies approved the scheme of merger on 10 July 2025.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. Applying the thresholds prescribed for enterprises operating only in India, the position is that-

options.A: the enterprise level threshold is crossed, the combined assets of ₹2,400 crore exceeding ₹2,000 crore
options.B: no threshold is crossed, the combined turnover of ₹5,200 crore falling short of ₹6,000 crore
options.C: no threshold is crossed, since both the assets test and the turnover test have to be satisfied
options.D: the enterprise level threshold is crossed only because neither party carries on business outside India

answer_html:
Answer: (A) the enterprise level threshold is crossed, the combined assets of ₹2,400 crore exceeding ₹2,000 crore.

For enterprises with a presence only in India the threshold is combined assets of more than ₹2,000 crore in India or combined turnover of more than ₹6,000 crore in India. The two tests are alternatives, so it is enough that the combined assets of ₹2,400 crore exceed ₹2,000 crore even though the combined turnover of ₹5,200 crore is below ₹6,000 crore.

Nilagiri Alloys Limited proposes to merge with Konkan Steel Products Limited. Both companies carry on business only in India and neither has any assets or any turnover outside India.

On the merger the combined assets of the two enterprises in India would be ₹2,400 crore and their combined turnover in India would be ₹5,200 crore.

The group to which the merged enterprise would belong after the merger would have assets in India of ₹7,600 crore and turnover in India of ₹25,200 crore.

The board of directors of each of the two companies approved the scheme of merger on 10 July 2025.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. Notice of the proposed combination has to be given to the Commission-

options.A: within 30 days of the order of the Tribunal sanctioning the scheme of merger of the two enterprises
options.B: within 7 days of the approval of the proposal for merger by the boards of directors of the enterprises
options.C: within 30 days of the approval of the proposal for merger by the boards of directors of the enterprises
options.D: within 60 days of the approval of the proposal for merger by the boards of directors of the enterprises

answer_html:
Answer: (C) within 30 days of the approval of the proposal for merger by the boards of directors of the enterprises.

A person or enterprise proposing to enter into a combination must give notice to the Commission in the specified form, with the prescribed fee, disclosing the details of the proposed combination, within 30 days of approval of the proposal relating to the merger or amalgamation by the board of directors, or of the execution of any agreement or other document for acquisition. The period of 7 days applies to the separate filing to be made where shares are acquired by a public financial institution, foreign institutional investor, bank or venture capital fund under a loan or investment agreement.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
Nilagiri Alloys Limited proposes to merge with Konkan Steel Products Limited. Both companies carry on business only in India and neither has any assets or any turnover outside India.

On the merger the combined assets of the two enterprises in India would be ₹2,400 crore and their combined turnover in India would be ₹5,200 crore.

The group to which the merged enterprise would belong after the merger would have assets in India of ₹7,600 crore and turnover in India of ₹25,200 crore.

The board of directors of each of the two companies approved the scheme of merger on 10 July 2025.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. Applying the thresholds prescribed for a group with a presence only in India, the position is that-

options.A: the group threshold is not crossed, the group assets of ₹7,600 crore falling short of ₹8,000 crore
options.B: the group threshold is not crossed, because both the group assets and the group turnover tests fail
options.C: the group threshold is crossed only in consequence of the enterprise level threshold being crossed
options.D: the group threshold is also crossed, the group turnover of ₹25,200 crore exceeding ₹24,000 crore

answer_html:
Answer: (D) the group threshold is also crossed, the group turnover of ₹25,200 crore exceeding ₹24,000 crore.

For a group present only in India the threshold is assets of more than ₹8,000 crore in India or turnover of more than ₹24,000 crore in India. Here the group assets of ₹7,600 crore fall short of ₹8,000 crore, but the group turnover of ₹25,200 crore exceeds ₹24,000 crore, and because the tests are alternatives that is enough. The group and enterprise level tests operate independently of one another.

On the merger the combined assets of the two enterprises in India would be ₹2,400 crore and their combined turnover in India would be ₹5,200 crore.

The board of directors of each of the two companies approved the scheme of merger on 10 July 2025.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. Notice is duly given, the Commission proposes no modification and passes no order. The combination will be deemed to have been approved on the expiry of-

options.A: 30 days from the date on which the notice was given to the Commission
options.B: 210 days from the date on which the notice was given to the Commission
options.C: 180 days from the date on which the notice was given to the Commission
options.D: one year from the date on which the combination has taken effect in law

answer_html:
Answer: (B) 210 days from the date on which the notice was given to the Commission.

No combination comes into effect until 210 days have passed from the day on which notice was given to the Commission, or the Commission has passed orders, whichever is earlier. If on the expiry of 210 days from the date of the notice the Commission has passed no order or issued no direction, the combination is deemed to have been approved. In computing that period the thirty working days and the further thirty working days allowed to the parties in connection with a proposed modification are excluded. The period of one year is the outer limit for the Commission initiating an inquiry of its own motion after the combination has taken effect.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Competition Commission of India consists of-

options.A: a Chairperson and not less than two and not more than four other part-time Members
options.B: a Chairperson and as many Members as the Central Government may from time to time notify
options.C: a Chairperson and not less than two and not more than six other whole-time Members
options.D: a Chairperson and not less than three and not more than eight other whole-time Members

answer_html:
Answer: (C) a Chairperson and not less than two and not more than six other whole-time Members.

The Commission consists of a Chairperson and not less than two and not more than six other Members, all of whom are whole-time and are appointed by the Central Government. Each must be a person of ability, integrity and standing with special knowledge of, and professional experience in, international trade, economics, business, commerce, law, finance, accountancy, management, industry, public affairs or competition matters.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Competition Commission of India is a body corporate with its head office at-

options.A: New Delhi
options.B: Mumbai
options.C: Kolkata
options.D: Bengaluru

answer_html:
Answer: (A) New Delhi.

The Central Government has established the Competition Commission of India as a body corporate headquartered at New Delhi. It was established with effect from 14 October 2003, and the provisions of the Act relating to anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominant position were notified on 20 May 2009.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Chairperson and every other Member of the Commission holds office for-

options.A: a term of 6 years, is eligible for one re-appointment, and retires at the age of 70 years
options.B: a term of 5 years, is eligible for re-appointment, and retires at the age of 65 years
options.C: a term of 3 years, is eligible for re-appointment, and retires at the age of 62 years
options.D: a term of 5 years, is not eligible for re-appointment, and retires at the age of 60 years

answer_html:
Answer: (B) a term of 5 years, is eligible for re-appointment, and retires at the age of 65 years.

The Chairperson and every other Member holds office for a term of 5 years from the date on which he enters upon office and is eligible for re-appointment. The age of retirement is 65 years. The Central Government may also appoint a Director General to assist the Commission in conducting inquiries into contraventions of the Act.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Where an agreement referred to in Section 3 has been entered into by a cartel, the Commission may impose on each producer, seller, distributor, trader or service provider in that cartel a penalty of up to-

options.A: two times its profit for each year of the continuance of the agreement, or five per cent of its turnover for each such year, whichever is higher
options.B: one per cent of the total turnover or of the assets of the enterprise for each year of the continuance of the agreement complained of
options.C: three times its profit for each year of the continuance of the agreement, or ten per cent of its turnover for each such year, whichever is higher
options.D: three times its profit for each year of the continuance of the agreement, or ten per cent of its turnover for each such year, whichever is lower

answer_html:
Answer: (C) three times its profit for each year of the continuance of the agreement, or ten per cent of its turnover for each such year, whichever is higher.

On finding a contravention the Commission may direct the enterprises to discontinue and not to re-enter the agreement, and may impose such penalty as it deems fit. Where the agreement has been entered into by a cartel the penalty on each member may extend to three times its profit for each year of the continuance of the agreement, or ten per cent of its turnover for each such year, whichever is higher.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Commission may impose a lesser penalty on a person who has made a full and true disclosure in respect of an alleged violation. That benefit is not available where-

options.A: the cartel has already continued for more than one year before the disclosure is made to the Commission
options.B: the Commission has already initiated an inquiry on its own motion before the disclosure is made to it
options.C: the report of the investigation directed under Section 26 has been received before the disclosure is made
options.D: the person making the disclosure is a producer rather than a seller, distributor or trader within the cartel

answer_html:
Answer: (C) the report of the investigation directed under Section 26 has been received before the disclosure is made.

A lesser penalty may be imposed where the Commission is satisfied that the person has made a full and true disclosure in respect of the alleged violations, but not where the report of the investigation directed under Section 26 has been received before the disclosure is made, and not where the person making the disclosure does not continue to co-operate until the proceedings are complete. If the condition on which the lesser penalty was imposed is not complied with, or false evidence is given, or the disclosure turns out not to be vital, the person may be tried and made liable to the penalty he would have borne.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Commission determines the relevant product market on the basis of-

options.A: the level of combination in the market, the extent of barriers to entry and the possibility of a failing business
options.B: physical characteristics or end-use, price, consumer preferences, exclusion of in-house production and specialised producers
options.C: regulatory trade barriers, local specification requirements, national procurement policies, transport costs and language
options.D: the market share, size and resources of the enterprise and the dependence of consumers on that particular enterprise

answer_html:
Answer: (B) physical characteristics or end-use, price, consumer preferences, exclusion of in-house production and specialised producers.

The relevant product market is determined on the basis of physical characteristics or end-use of goods, the price of goods or services, consumer preferences, exclusion of in-house production, the existence of specialised producers and the classification of industrial products. The factors in the second option are those for the relevant geographic market; those in the third go to dominance; and those in the fourth go to the appreciable adverse effect of a combination.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: A person who without reasonable cause fails to comply with an order of the Commission, and a person who fails to comply with a direction of the Director General, are each punishable with a fine of ₹1 lakh for each day of default, subject to a maximum of-

options.A: ₹1 crore in the first case and ₹10 crore in the second
options.B: ₹10 crore in both of the two cases, the provisions being identical
options.C: ₹1 crore in both of the two cases, the provisions being identical
options.D: ₹10 crore in the first case and ₹1 crore in the second

answer_html:
Answer: (D) ₹10 crore in the first case and ₹1 crore in the second.

Failure without reasonable cause to comply with the orders or directions of the Commission attracts a fine which may extend to ₹1 lakh for each day during which the non-compliance continues, subject to a maximum of ₹10 crore, and continued default may be punished with imprisonment. Failure to comply with a direction of the Commission under Section 36 or of the Director General under Section 41 attracts the same daily fine but is subject to a maximum of ₹1 crore.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: An appeal against a direction, decision or order of the Commission lies to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal within 60 days, and a further appeal against an order of that Tribunal lies-

options.A: to the Central Government within thirty days of communication of the order of the Tribunal
options.B: to the Competition Commission of India itself, sitting in review of its own earlier decision
options.C: to the Supreme Court within sixty days of communication of the order of the Appellate Tribunal
options.D: to the jurisdictional High Court within ninety days of communication of the order of the Tribunal

answer_html:
Answer: (C) to the Supreme Court within sixty days of communication of the order of the Appellate Tribunal.

The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal constituted under Section 410 of the Companies Act, 2013 is the Appellate Tribunal for the purposes of this Act, and an aggrieved person may appeal to it within 60 days of receiving a copy of the direction, decision or order. The Central Government, a State Government, the Commission, a statutory or local authority, an enterprise or any aggrieved person may then appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days of communication of the decision or order of the Appellate Tribunal.
